claim: The axon initial segment (AIS) constitutes the site of action potential initiation.
source: The axon initial segment (AIS) constitutes not only the site of action potential initiation, but also a hub for activity-dependent modulation of output generation.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience, supported by the manuscript's introduction and cited literature.

claim: The AIS is a hub for activity-dependent modulation of output generation.
source: The axon initial segment (AIS) constitutes not only the site of action potential initiation, but also a hub for activity-dependent modulation of output generation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the introduction's discussion of AIS plasticity.

claim: No robust murine in vivo live reporters for the AIS existed prior to this study.
source: Recent studies shedding light on AIS function used predominantly post-hoc approaches since no robust murine in vivo live reporters exist.
evidence: This claim is made in the abstract to establish the novelty of the work.

claim: The ankyrin-G-GFP reporter line is activated by Cre recombinase.
source: Here, we introduce a reporter line in which the AIS is intrinsically labeled by an ankyrin-G-GFP fusion protein activated by Cre recombinase, tagging the native Ank3 gene.
evidence: This is the core description of the mouse model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The subcellular scaffold of the AIS remains unchanged in ankyrin-G-GFP labeled cells.
source: Using confocal, superresolution, and two-photon microscopy as well as whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo, we confirm that the subcellular scaffold of the AIS and electrophysiological parameters of labeled cells remain unchanged.
evidence: This is confirmed through multiple experimental approaches described in the manuscript.

claim: Electrophysiological parameters of ankyrin-G-GFP labeled cells remain unchanged.
source: Using confocal, superresolution, and two-photon microscopy as well as whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo, we confirm that the subcellular scaffold of the AIS and electrophysiological parameters of labeled cells remain unchanged.
evidence: This is demonstrated through patch-clamp recordings comparing control and ankyrin-G-GFP expressing neurons.

claim: Rapid AIS remodeling occurs following increased network activity in the ankyrin-G-GFP model system.
source: We further uncover rapid AIS remodeling following increased network activity in this model system, as well as highly reproducible in vivo labeling of AIS over weeks.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with KCl application in acute slices.

claim: In vivo labeling of AIS is highly reproducible over weeks in the ankyrin-G-GFP model.
source: We further uncover rapid AIS remodeling following increased network activity in this model system, as well as highly reproducible in vivo labeling of AIS over weeks.
evidence: This is shown through longitudinal two-photon imaging experiments.

claim: The AIS is the cellular compartment where most neurons integrate synaptic input and generate action potentials.
source: The AIS is the cellular compartment where most neurons integrate synaptic input and generate their primary output signal, the action potential (AP); (Bender and Trussell, 2012; Kole and Stuart, 2012).
evidence: This is a fundamental statement about AIS function supported by citations.

claim: The AIS is critical for the initiation of action potentials.
source: It is critical for the initiation of APs and receives input from specialized inhibitory neurons which enables synchronization of neuronal firing across nearby cells (Wefelmeyer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citation.

claim: The AIS receives input from specialized inhibitory neurons which enables synchronization of neuronal firing across nearby cells.
source: It is critical for the initiation of APs and receives input from specialized inhibitory neurons which enables synchronization of neuronal firing across nearby cells (Wefelmeyer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The AIS responds to changes in neuronal activity with homeostatic plasticity defined by structural changes in AIS length, position, and channel architecture.
source: Much like synapses, the AIS responds to changes in neuronal activity with different types of homeostatic plasticity, defined by structural changes in AIS length, position, and channel architecture (Jamann et al., 2021; Grubb and Burrone, 2010; Kuba et al., 2010; Zbili et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Most recent studies investigating AIS function and plasticity relied on ex vivo immunofluorescent staining in fixed neuronal tissue and cultures.
source: Most recent studies investigating AIS function and plasticity relied on ex vivo immunofluorescent staining in fixed neuronal tissue and cultures using antibodies against elements of the AIS cytoskeleton and post-hoc analysis.
evidence: This describes the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: Ankyrin-G and βIV-spectrin cluster voltage-gated ion channels at the AIS.
source: These targets make sense, since the scaffolding proteins ankyrin-G and βIV-spectrin cluster voltage-gated ion channels at the AIS and provide a cellular anchor between the axonal membrane and cytoskeleton (Jenkins et al., 2015; Leterrier et al., 2015; Leterrier et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Ankyrin-G and βIV-spectrin provide a cellular anchor between the axonal membrane and cytoskeleton.
source: These targets make sense, since the scaffolding proteins ankyrin-G and βIV-spectrin cluster voltage-gated ion channels at the AIS and provide a cellular anchor between the axonal membrane and cytoskeleton (Jenkins et al., 2015; Leterrier et al., 2015; Leterrier et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Live labeling of the AIS can be achieved using antibodies against the extracellular domain protein neurofascin-186.
source: Recent approaches allow for live labeling of the AIS using antibodies against the extracellular domain protein neurofascin-186 (Dumitrescu et al., 2016) or by transfecting cultured primary neurons with ankyrin-G-GFP constructs (Komada and Soriano, 2002).
evidence: This describes existing approaches with citations.

claim: Live labeling of the AIS can be achieved by transfecting cultured primary neurons with ankyrin-G-GFP constructs.
source: Recent approaches allow for live labeling of the AIS using antibodies against the extracellular domain protein neurofascin-186 (Dumitrescu et al., 2016) or by transfecting cultured primary neurons with ankyrin-G-GFP constructs (Komada and Soriano, 2002).
evidence: This describes existing approaches with citations.

claim: Ankyrin-G and βIV-spectrin are large proteins that are difficult to express.
source: For example, ankyrin-G and βIV-spectrin are large proteins that are, therefore, difficult to express (Jenkins et al., 2015; Komada and Soriano, 2002; Berghs et al., 2000) and their overexpression, when successful, may conceivably have an altering impact on AIS architecture and/or function.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Overexpression of ankyrin-G and βIV-spectrin may have an altering impact on AIS architecture and/or function.
source: For example, ankyrin-G and βIV-spectrin are large proteins that are, therefore, difficult to express (Jenkins et al., 2015; Komada and Soriano, 2002; Berghs et al., 2000) and their overexpression, when successful, may conceivably have an altering impact on AIS architecture and/or function.
evidence: This is a concern raised about existing approaches.

claim: All currently available live reporters for the AIS are solely established for in vitro applications.
source: Also, all currently available live reporters are solely established for in vitro applications.
evidence: This describes a limitation of existing approaches.

claim: Previous studies on AIS plasticity combined electrophysiological recordings with post-hoc immunostainings, preventing longitudinal tracking of AIS plasticity in the same cells over time.
source: Other studies uncovering the role of the AIS in the modulation of neuronal excitability combined electrophysiological recordings with post-hoc immunostainings (Grubb and Burrone, 2010; Kuba et al., 2010; Wefelmeyer et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2019), preventing longitudinal tracking of AIS plasticity in the same cells over time.
evidence: This describes a limitation of previous approaches with citations.

claim: The ankyrin-G-GFP mouse line was generated using the native Ank3 locus.
source: To overcome these limitations, we have generated a mouse line for Cre-dependent expression of an ankyrin-G-GFP fusion protein using the native Ank3 locus.
evidence: This describes the generation of the mouse model.

claim: The ankyrin-G-GFP mouse line allows monitoring of AIS parameters in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo.
source: This novel mouse line allows the monitoring of AIS parameters in vitro (isolated cells, organotypic cultures, OTC), ex vivo (acute brain slices), and in vivo (living mice).
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the mouse model.

claim: The ankyrin-G-GFP model demonstrates efficient labeling of AIS and nodes of Ranvier in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo.
source: Using this model, we demonstrate efficient labeling of AIS and nodes of Ranvier (noR) in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo by expression of Cre recombinase.
evidence: This is a key finding demonstrated throughout the results section.

claim: The Cre-dependence of the ankyrin-G-GFP model allows labeling of the AIS and noR in genetically defined neuronal populations.
source: The Cre-dependence of this model allows labeling of the AIS and noR in genetically defined neuronal populations and with temporal precision in the living animal or acute slice, depending on the selected Cre-line or Cre-supplementing virus.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model.

claim: Ankyrin-G-GFP mice have normal AIS properties, including clustering of binding partners.
source: We show that ankyrin-G-GFP mice have normal AIS properties, including clustering of binding partners, inhibitory synaptic clustering, and nanostructure.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunostaining experiments.

claim: Ankyrin-G-GFP mice have normal inhibitory synaptic clustering at the AIS.
source: We show that ankyrin-G-GFP mice have normal AIS properties, including clustering of binding partners, inhibitory synaptic clustering, and nanostructure.
evidence: This is demonstrated through vGAT staining experiments.

claim: Ankyrin-G-GFP mice have normal AIS nanostructure.
source: We show that ankyrin-G-GFP mice have normal AIS properties, including clustering of binding partners, inhibitory synaptic clustering, and nanostructure.
evidence: This is demonstrated through STED microscopy experiments.

claim: The electrophysiological properties of ankyrin-G-GFP neurons are indistinguishable from those found in wild-type littermate controls.
source: In addition, we demonstrate that the electrophysiological properties of ankyrin-G-GFP neurons are indistinguishable from those found in wild-type littermate controls, including AP properties and excitatory synaptic function.
evidence: This is demonstrated through patch-clamp recordings.

claim: AIS plasticity can be demonstrated in organotypic tissue cultures from ankyrin-G-GFP mice.
source: In a proof-of-principle approach, we further demonstrate AIS plasticity in OTC from ankyrin-G-GFP mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with MgSO4 and KCl treatments.

claim: AIS can be imaged in vivo with two-photon microscopy in both superficial and deep brain regions.
source: Finally, we show that AIS can be imaged in vivo with two-photon microscopy in both superficial and deep brain regions and that the ankyrin-G-GFP-labeled AIS can be imaged over days and weeks.
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vivo imaging experiments.

claim: Ankyrin-G-GFP-labeled AIS can be imaged over days and weeks in vivo.
source: Finally, we show that AIS can be imaged in vivo with two-photon microscopy in both superficial and deep brain regions and that the ankyrin-G-GFP-labeled AIS can be imaged over days and weeks.
evidence: This is demonstrated through longitudinal imaging experiments.

claim: Ankyrin-G is an intracellular scaffolding protein critical for the formation and maintenance of the AIS.
source: Ankyrin-G is an intracellular scaffolding protein critical for the formation and maintenance of the AIS, where it recruits multiple cytoskeletal elements, ion channels, transporters, and cell adhesion molecules that are necessary for normal AIS function (Nelson and Jenkins, 2017; Rasband, 2010; Leterrier, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Ankyrin-G recruits multiple cytoskeletal elements, ion channels, transporters, and cell adhesion molecules at the AIS.
source: Ankyrin-G is an intracellular scaffolding protein critical for the formation and maintenance of the AIS, where it recruits multiple cytoskeletal elements, ion channels, transporters, and cell adhesion molecules that are necessary for normal AIS function (Nelson and Jenkins, 2017; Rasband, 2010; Leterrier, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Ankyrin-G tolerates the addition of a GFP tag.
source: Ankyrin-G tolerates the addition of a GFP tag, since ankyrin-G-GFP can rescue multiple functions of ankyrin-G in Ank3 null neurons, including scaffolding of voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, clustering of the spectrin cytoskeleton, and recruitment of inhibitory synapses (Jenkins et al., 2015; Fréal et al., 2016; Tseng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations from previous studies.

claim: Ankyrin-G-GFP can rescue multiple functions of ankyrin-G in Ank3 null neurons, including scaffolding of voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels.
source: Ankyrin-G tolerates the addition of a GFP tag, since ankyrin-G-GFP can rescue multiple functions of ankyrin-G in Ank3 null neurons, including scaffolding of voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, clustering of the spectrin cytoskeleton, and recruitment of inhibitory synapses (Jenkins et al., 2015; Fréal et al., 2016; Tseng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations from previous studies.

claim: Ankyrin-G-GFP can rescue clustering of the spectrin cytoskeleton in Ank3 null neurons.
source: Ankyrin-G tolerates the addition of a GFP tag, since ankyrin-G-GFP can rescue multiple functions of ankyrin-G in Ank3 null neurons, including scaffolding of voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, clustering of the spectrin cytoskeleton, and recruitment of inhibitory synapses (Jenkins et al., 2015; Fréal et al., 2016; Tseng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations from previous studies.

claim: Ankyrin-G-GFP can rescue recruitment of inhibitory synapses in Ank3 null neurons.
source: Ankyrin-G tolerates the addition of a GFP tag, since ankyrin-G-GFP can rescue multiple functions of ankyrin-G in Ank3 null neurons, including scaffolding of voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, clustering of the spectrin cytoskeleton, and recruitment of inhibitory synapses (Jenkins et al., 2015; Fréal et al., 2016; Tseng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations from previous studies.

claim: A FLEx cassette system was used to flip out the last exon of Ank3 and replace it with the last exon of Ank3 fused with the coding sequence for GFP.
source: To intrinsically label ankyrin-G with GFP, we utilized a FLEx cassette system to flip out the last exon of Ank3 and replace it with the last exon of Ank3 fused with the coding sequence for GFP (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the genetic engineering strategy used to create the mouse line, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: Constitutive tagging of the endogenous Ank3 allele would make it difficult to visualize ankyrin-G-dependent structures due to heterogeneous expression of ankyrin-G in various cell compartments across multiple tissues.
source: Given the heterogeneous expression of ankyrin-G in various cell compartments across multiple tissues, constitutive tagging of the endogenous Ank3 allele would make it difficult to visualize ankyrin-G-dependent structures.
evidence: This explains the rationale for using a conditional system.

claim: The conditional system allows GFP-labeling of ankyrin-G only in cells expressing Cre recombinase.
source: By contrast, our system allows us to only GFP-label ankyrin-G in cells expressing Cre recombinase, allowing the visualization of ankyrin-G in genetically and temporally defined cell populations.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the system.

claim: The linker-GFP sequence used in the ankyrin-G-GFP mouse is from rescue plasmids used in multiple studies to examine the function of the three main classes of brain ankyrin-G isoforms (190, 270, and 480 kDa).
source: To this end, we utilized the linker-GFP sequence from the rescue plasmids used in multiple studies from our group and others to examine the function of the three main classes of brain ankyrin-G isoforms, 190, 270, and 480 kDa, respectively.
evidence: This describes the source of the linker-GFP sequence.

claim: GFP fusions of ankyrin-G have been shown to be sufficient to rescue Ank3 knockout or silencing in the formation of the AIS, noR, GABAergic synapses, and dendritic spines.
source: Importantly, these GFP fusions have been shown to be sufficient to rescue Ank3 knockout or silencing in the formation of the AIS, noR, GABAergic synapses, and dendritic spines (Jenkins et al., 2015; Fréal et al., 2016; Tseng et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations from previous studies.

claim: Hippocampal organotypic cultures from ank-G-GFP mice exposed to AAV expressing Cre-recombinase showed GFP expression along the AIS after 48 hours.
source: Ank-G-GFP mice were first used to generate hippocampal OTC, which were then exposed to AAV expressing Cre-recombinase under the control of the synapsin promotor (AAV5-pmSyn1-EBFP-Cre). After 48 hr, neurons exposed to the virus showed GFP expression along their AIS (Figure 2B, left panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Not all AIS in organotypic culture neurons were GFP+, likely due to the transfection efficiency with AAV-Cre.
source: Not all AIS in OTC neurons were GFP+, likely due to the transfection efficiency with AAV-Cre.
evidence: This is an observation from the OTC experiments with an inference about the cause.

claim: The somatic envelope and proximal dendrites were visible via the ank-G-GFP signal.
source: Of note, the somatic envelope and proximal dendrites were also visible via the ank-G-GFP signal (Figure 2C, asterisks in left panel), highlighting ankyrin-G expression in the somatodendritic compartment of mature neurons (Tseng et al., 2015; Nelson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with supporting citations.

claim: Ankyrin-G is expressed in the somatodendritic compartment of mature neurons.
source: Of note, the somatic envelope and proximal dendrites were also visible via the ank-G-GFP signal (Figure 2C, asterisks in left panel), highlighting ankyrin-G expression in the somatodendritic compartment of mature neurons (Tseng et al., 2015; Nelson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Ank-G-GFP reporter expression always colocalized with βIV-spectrin and ankyrin-G markers.
source: In all experiments outlined above, double labeling against the characteristic AIS markers βIV-spectrin and ankyrin-G, respectively, served as control of AIS identity of labeled structures and we found that ank-G-GFP reporter expression always colocalized with these markers.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the validation experiments.

claim: The 480 kDa isoform of ankyrin-G is localized to nodes of Ranvier in myelinated axons.
source: The 480 kDa isoform of ankyrin-G is also localized to nodes of Ranvier (noR) in myelinated axons where it serves as a scaffold for voltage-gated ion channels similar to those found at the AIS (Jenkins et al., 2015; Jenkins and Bennett, 2002; Dzhashiashvili et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The 480 kDa isoform of ankyrin-G serves as a scaffold for voltage-gated ion channels at nodes of Ranvier.
source: The 480 kDa isoform of ankyrin-G is also localized to nodes of Ranvier (noR) in myelinated axons where it serves as a scaffold for voltage-gated ion channels similar to those found at the AIS (Jenkins et al., 2015; Jenkins and Bennett, 2002; Dzhashiashvili et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: In ank-G-GFP × CaMKIIa-Cre mice, nodes of Ranvier in the alveus of hippocampal CA3 were visible as distinct puncta that co-localized with ankyrin-G and Nav1.6.
source: In mice expressing ank-G-GFP in CaMKIIa-positive excitatory neurons, noR in the alveus of hippocampal CA3 were visible as distinct puncta that co-localized with other nodal markers such as ankyrin-G and Nav1.6 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Only CaMKII-expressing neurons showed ank-G-GFP signals in nodes of Ranvier.
source: Of note, only CaMKII-expressing neurons showed ank-G-GFP signals in noR (Figure 3A, green circles).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ank-G-GFP– nodes of Ranvier were characterized by the colocalization of ankyrin-G and Nav1.6.
source: Ank-G-GFP– noR were still characterized by the colocalization of ankyrin-G and Nav1.6 (Figure 3A, blue circles).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Immunostaining against GFP, ankyrin-G, and Caspr revealed normal localization of ank-G-GFP and Caspr to the node and paranode, respectively, in myelinated axons of CaMKII-positive neurons.
source: Immunostaining against GFP, ankyrin-G, and Caspr revealed normal localization of ank-G-GFP and Caspr to the node and paranode, respectively, in myelinated axons of CaMKII-positive neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Node shape and fluorescence signals of Nav1.6 and ankyrin-G showed no differences between GFP+ and GFP- nodes.
source: The quantification of node shape and fluorescence signals of Nav1.6 and ankyrin-G showed no differences between GFP+ and GFP- nodes (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: GFP label intensities within GFP+ nodes did not interfere with Nav1.6 levels.
source: Furthermore, GFP label intensities within GFP+ nodes did not interfere with Nav1.6 levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, top panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a strong correlation between GFP and ankyrin-G in GFP+ nodes.
source: Instead, we found a strong correlation between GFP and ankyrin-G in GFP+ nodes, demonstrating the specificity of our model (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, bottom panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The length and distance of AIS (measured by βIV-spectrin signal) did not differ between neighboring GFP+ and GFP- CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: We found that the length and distance of AIS (measured by βIV-spectrin signal) did not differ between neighboring GFP+ and GFP- CA1 pyramidal cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Length measurements using the live ankyrin-GFP label in combination with post-fixed ankyrin-G or βIV-spectrin of the same AIS showed a strong correlation with one another.
source: Length measurements using the live ankyrin-GFP label in combination with post-fixed ankyrin-G or βIV-spectrin of the same AIS showed a strong correlation with one another (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Colabeling of Nav1.6 with βIV-spectrin in ank-G-GFP+ AIS showed homogeneous signals of Nav1.6 across the length of neighboring GFP+ and GFP- AIS.
source: Colabeling of the sodium channel isoform Nav1.6 with βIV-spectrin in ank-G-GFP+ AIS in cortical layer V pyramidal neurons showed homogeneous signals of Nav1.6 across the length of neighboring GFP+ and GFP- AIS.
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A similar expression of Kv2.1 was observed in GFP+ and GFP- AIS.
source: Likewise, a similar expression of Kv2.1 was observed in GFP+ and GFP- AIS (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Neurofascin-186 is important for the recruitment of ion channels to the AIS during development.
source: The AIS is also characterized by the expression of several cell adhesion molecules, chief among them neurofascin-186 (NF-186), which is important for the recruitment of ion channels to the AIS during development (Hedstrom et al., 2007; Alpizar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Immunostaining against NF-186 in ank-G-GFP+ AIS produced the expected co-staining pattern.
source: Potential disruption of normal AIS assembly in our reporter model may have an impact on the assembly of the extracellular niche at the AIS, however, immunostaining against NF-186 in ank-G-GFP+ AIS produced the expected co-staining pattern (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TRIM46 organizes the fasciculation of microtubules in the AIS.
source: The AIS-related proteins TRIM46, organizing the fasciculation of microtubules in the AIS (Fréal et al., 2019; Harterink et al., 2019) and FGF14, regulating voltage-gated ion channels at the AIS (Pablo and Pitt, 2017), were also detected in ank-G-GFP+ neurons throughout the neocortex of ank-G-GFP x CaMKII-Cre mice (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: FGF14 regulates voltage-gated ion channels at the AIS.
source: The AIS-related proteins TRIM46, organizing the fasciculation of microtubules in the AIS (Fréal et al., 2019; Harterink et al., 2019) and FGF14, regulating voltage-gated ion channels at the AIS (Pablo and Pitt, 2017), were also detected in ank-G-GFP+ neurons throughout the neocortex of ank-G-GFP x CaMKII-Cre mice (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: TRIM46 and FGF14 were detected in ank-G-GFP+ neurons throughout the neocortex of ank-G-GFP x CaMKII-Cre mice.
source: The AIS-related proteins TRIM46, organizing the fasciculation of microtubules in the AIS (Fréal et al., 2019; Harterink et al., 2019) and FGF14, regulating voltage-gated ion channels at the AIS (Pablo and Pitt, 2017), were also detected in ank-G-GFP+ neurons throughout the neocortex of ank-G-GFP x CaMKII-Cre mice (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Synaptopodin has been shown to be a reliable and reproducible marker for the cisternal organelle in the AIS.
source: The actin-binding protein synaptopodin (synpo) has been shown to be a reliable and reproducible marker for the CO in the AIS (Hanemaaijer, 2020; Schlüter et al., 2017; Sánchez-Ponce et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Immunostaining with antibodies against GFP, synpo, and βIV-spectrin revealed labeling of the cisternal organelle within the AIS of ank-G-GFP+-neurons.
source: Immunostaining with antibodies against GFP, synpo, and βIV-spectrin in layer V pyramidal neurons of primary motor cortex of ank-G-GFP x CaMKII-Cre mice revealed labeling of the CO within the AIS of ank-G-GFP+-neurons (Figure 5A) with the typical synpo+ spine apparatus as part of the dendritic domain visible in all samples (Figure 5A, magenta puncta in the background).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No significant difference in synaptopodin cluster number per AIS was observed between GFP- and GFP+ AIS from ank-G-GFP x CaMKII-Cre mice.
source: To test whether GFP-expression had an impact on the normal distribution of synpo clusters in pyramidal neurons, we quantified cluster number per AIS and compared GFP- and GFP+ AIS from the same ank-G-GFP x CaMKII-Cre mice. No significant difference between GFP- and GFP+ AIS was observed (GFP- AIS 3.1±1.7 clusters vs GFP+ 3.3±1.7 clusters; n=50 AIS from three animals, p=0.6444, unpaired t-test; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A with statistical analysis.

claim: Ank-G-GFP+-AIS were contacted by vGAT+ axo-axonic interneurons.
source: Data revealed that indeed, ank-G-GFP+-AIS were contacted by vGAT+ axo-axonic interneurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No significant difference in the number of vGAT+ puncta along AIS was found between GFP- and GFP+ AIS from ank-G-GFP x CaMKII-Cre mice.
source: Therefore, we quantified the number of vGAT+ puncta along GFP- and GFP+ AIS from the same ank-G-GFP x CaMKII-Cre mice. We found no significant difference between these groups (GFP- AIS 20.7±2.3 vGAT puncta vs GFP+ 20.8±2.2 vGAT puncta; n=50 AIS from three animals, p=0.7917, unpaired t-test; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claim: Approximately 4% of all AIS in rodent cortex are ensheathed in microglial processes.
source: A further characteristic of the AIS is its occasional ensheathing in microglial processes, which is the case for approximately 4% of all AIS in rodent cortex (Baalman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Scarce, but clearly distinguishable interaction of select GFP+ AIS with microglial processes was found in S1 layer II/III pyramidal neurons of ank-G-GFP × CaMKII mice.
source: We, therefore, performed immunostaining against the microglial marker Iba1 in ank-G-GFP × CaMKII mice and found scarce, but clearly distinguishable interaction of select GFP+ AIS with microglial processes in S1 layer II/III pyramidal neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The nanostructure of the AIS scaffold in cortical neurons exhibits a stereotypical subcellular organization with a periodic spacing of actin and spectrin rings intercalating with voltage-gated ion channels at approximately 170–190 nm distance.
source: The nanostructure of the AIS scaffold in cortical neurons exhibits a stereotypical subcellular organization, in which a periodic spacing of actin and spectrin rings intercalates with voltage-gated ion channels at approximately 170–190 nm distance, depending on the cell type studied (Leterrier et al., 2015; Schlüter et al., 2019; Akter et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Both concentration and spatial arrangement of ion channels are thought to be crucial for action potential generation and modulation.
source: Both concentration and spatial arrangement of ion channels are thought to be crucial for AP generation and modulation (Lazarov et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2009; Inda et al., 2006; Kress et al., 2010) and, therefore, constitute a hallmark of excitable neuronal microdomains such as the AIS.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Autocorrelation analysis verified the characteristic 190 nm periodic organization of ankyrin-G, βIV-spectrin, and Kv1.2.
source: Autocorrelation analysis verified the characteristic 190 nm periodic organization of the proteins investigated (Figure 6C; left = ankyrin G, middle = βIV-spectrin, right = Kv1.2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Autocorrelation amplitude analysis showed no significant difference between untreated, ΔCre or +Cre ank-G-GFP cultures for ankyrin-G, βIV-spectrin, and Kv1.2.
source: Further, an autocorrelation amplitude analysis, which calculates the difference between the autocorrelation value at 190 nm and the average values at 95 nm and 285 nm, respectively, was performed, showing no significant difference between untreated, ΔCre or +Cre ank-G-GFP cultures (Figure 6D; left = ankyrin G, middle = βIV-spectrin, right = Kv1.2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Ank-G-GFP+-AIS develop normally and upon Cre-activation, retain their nanoscale organization.
source: In summary, our data indicate that ank-G-GFP+-AIS develop normally and upon Cre-activation, retain their nanoscale organization.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the STED microscopy data.

claim: Passive membrane properties such as resting membrane potential and input resistance showed no significant difference between neurons expressing Cre-recombinase and ΔCre controls in dissociated hippocampal neurons.
source: In dissociated hippocampal neurons, we first determined passive membrane properties such as resting membrane potential (RMP) and input resistance (Rs) and found no significant difference between neurons expressing Cre-recombinase and ΔCre controls (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Action potential properties, including amplitude, half-width, voltage threshold, maximum rise time, and rheobase were unaffected by the GFP fusion construct in dissociated hippocampal neurons.
source: Similarly, AP properties, including amplitude, half-width, voltage threshold, maximum rise time, and rheobase were unaffected (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The input/output relation and maximum slope f' (max) of the I/F-curve provided evidence that the GFP fusion construct does not alter the firing properties of infected neurons in vitro.
source: Plotting the input/output relation with a comparison of the maximum slope f' (max) of the I/F-curve further provided evidence that the GFP fusion construct does not alter the firing properties of infected neurons in vitro.
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: No evidence of an impact of the GFP fusion protein on passive and active properties was found in ex vivo hippocampal acute slices from wild-type mice, ank-G-GFP mice without Cre exposure, and ank-G-GFP x CamKII-Cre mice.
source: The same electrophysiological parameters were tested in ex vivo hippocampal acute slices from three groups: (i) wild-type mice, (ii) ank-G-GFP mice without Cre exposure, and (iii) ank-G-GFP x CamKII-Cre mice (Figure 7C and D). We found no evidence of an impact of the GFP fusion protein on any of the investigated passive and active properties (Figure 7C and D, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: AIS elongation is a process that requires a longer time frame of network silencing (days to weeks).
source: Since previous research indicated that AIS elongation is a process that requires a longer time frame of network silencing (days to weeks; Jamann et al., 2021; Gutzmann et al., 2014), we first blocked synaptic transmission via NMDA receptors by maintaining OTC in the presence of 10 mM MgSO4 for 20 d.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Under conditions of blocked synaptic transmission (10 mM MgSO4 for 20 days), AIS elongated significantly in organotypic cultures.
source: Under these conditions, AIS elongated significantly (Ctrl 27.9±3.0 µm vs MgSO4 32.1±2.4 µm, n=6 OTC, 50 AIS per OTC; Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A and B with statistical analysis.

claim: The same AIS elongation effect was observed when cultures were maintained in MgSO4 for 10 days.
source: The same effect was observed when cultures were maintained in MgSO4 for 10 d (Ctrl 32.1±3.5 µm vs MgSO4 35.9±1.2 µm, n=6 OTC, 50 AIS per OTC; Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C with statistical analysis.

claim: Induction of increased network activity by exposing organotypic cultures to chronic depolarizing conditions (6 mM KCl) for 20 days and 10 days did not result in significant AIS length changes.
source: Induction of increased network activity by exposing OTC to chronic depolarizing conditions (6 mM KCl) for 20 d and 10 d, respectively, did not result in significant length changes (KCl(10 d) 29.9±1.8 µm, KCl(20 d) 27.0±2.7 µm, n=6 OTC, 50 AIS per OTC; Figure 8B and D, one-way ANOVA and Tukey's test for B, unpaired t-tests for C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B and D with statistical analysis.

claim: AIS length returned to baseline after rescue conditions (normal growth medium) following initial exposure to MgSO4 for 10 days.
source: In MgSO4-treated OCT, AIS length returned to baseline after rescue (Ctrl MgSO4 27.9±3.0 µm vs rescue 30.6±2.3 µm; n=6 OTC, 50 AIS per OTC; Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C with statistical analysis.

claim: Rescue paradigms in KCl-treated cultures did not affect AIS length.
source: Rescue paradigms in KCl-treated cultures did not affect AIS length as expected (Ctrl KCl 27.9±3.0 µm vs rescue 28.9±1.9 µm; n=6 OTC, 50 AIS per OTC; Figure 8D, all tests performed as unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8D with statistical analysis.

claim: AIS shortening after increased network activity occurs in a rapid time frame (1 hour) and is bidirectional with a return to baseline after an initial length change.
source: AIS shortening after increased network activity occurs in a rapid time frame (1 hour) and is bidirectional with a return to baseline after an initial length change (Jamann et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Direct application of high potassium (15 mM KCl) resulted in a relative length reduction only of the AIS associated with the affected neuron in acute slices.
source: Direct application of high potassium resulted in a relative length reduction only of the AIS associated with the affected neuron, while all surrounding labeled AIS maintained their initial length (n=4 pairs of sample and control AIS; 10 min Ctrl vs KCl: p=0.0068; 20 min Ctrl vs KCl: p=0.0045; 30 min Ctrl vs KCl: p=0.0130; paired t-tests, Figure 8E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8E with statistical analysis.

claim: Within minutes of KCl application to the axon hillock, partial disappearance of the proximal onset of an individual AIS was observed.
source: Interestingly, within minutes of the KCl application to the axon hillock, we observed the partial disappearance of the proximal onset of an individual AIS (Figure 8E, insets).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Actual structural AIS changes occur rapidly within 10 minutes and can be visualized and monitored within the same neuron.
source: We here demonstrate that actual structural AIS changes do occur rapidly within 10 min and that they can be visualized and monitored within the same neuron.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the rapid plasticity experiments.

claim: The same individual AIS maintained their average length reliably over a 7-day interval in vivo.
source: We compared the same region of interest at a 7 d interval and analyzed the length of the same individual AIS (Figure 9B and C). Quantification revealed that the same AIS maintained their average length reliably (week 1, magenta: 17.3±3.9 µm vs week 2, green: 16.8±3.9 µm, paired t-test, n=30 AIS; Figure 9B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B with statistical analysis.

claim: There is a strong and significant correlation among individual AIS lengths measured in the same region of interest from week 1 and week 2 in vivo.
source: Plotting of mean AIS length from week 1 and week 2 indicated a strong and significant correlation among individual AIS lengths measured in the same ROI (r2=0.7892, p<0.0001, n=30 AIS; Figure 9B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B with statistical analysis.

claim: AIS could be monitored in vivo in specific subpopulations of cross-callosal pyramidal neurons of the caudal forelimb region of M1 using a viral approach.
source: In addition to constitutive expression of ank-G-GFP in intercrossed transgenic mice, AIS could also be monitored in vivo using a viral approach in two additional systems: (1) specific subpopulations of cross-callosal pyramidal neurons of the caudal forelimb region of M1 (Figure 9D) and (2) principal neurons of deep brain areas, like the basolateral amygdala (BLA) via gradient reflective index (GRIN) lenses (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9D.

claim: AIS could be monitored in vivo in principal neurons of deep brain areas like the basolateral amygdala via GRIN lenses using a viral approach.
source: In addition to constitutive expression of ank-G-GFP in intercrossed transgenic mice, AIS could also be monitored in vivo using a viral approach in two additional systems: (1) specific subpopulations of cross-callosal pyramidal neurons of the caudal forelimb region of M1 (Figure 9D) and (2) principal neurons of deep brain areas, like the basolateral amygdala (BLA) via gradient reflective index (GRIN) lenses (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The ank-G-GFP model is a powerful tool to study excitable membrane domains in living animals in future studies of neural development, animal behavior, and disease progression.
source: Our live imaging data provides evidence that the ank-G-GFP model is a powerful tool to study excitable membrane domains in living animals in future studies of neural development, animal behavior, and disease progression.
evidence: This is a concluding statement based on the in vivo imaging data.

claim: An increasing number of studies have shown that neurons respond to changes in neuronal activity by altering the length, position, and/or channel distribution of the AIS.
source: An increasing number of studies have shown that neurons respond to changes in neuronal activity by altering the length, position, and/or channel distribution of the AIS (Wefelmeyer et al., 2016; Jamann et al., 2021; Grubb and Burrone, 2010; Kuba et al., 2010; Zbili et al., 2021; Yamada and Kuba, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Sensory deprivation elicits lengthening of the AIS and a corresponding increase in neuronal excitability in the barrel cortex.
source: For example, sensory deprivation elicits lengthening of the AIS and a corresponding increase in neuronal excitability in the barrel cortex (Jamann et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Conditions that mimic mild traumatic brain injury cause decreases in AIS length in the somatosensory cortex.
source: Conditions that mimic mild traumatic brain injury cause decreases in AIS length in the somatosensory cortex (Vascak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: AIS plasticity in response to changes in network activity has been observed in the avian and rodent auditory system.
source: AIS plasticity in response to changes in network activity has further been observed in the avian (Kuba et al., 2010) and rodent auditory system (Kim et al., 2019), isolated hippocampal neurons (Grubb and Burrone, 2010), hippocampal OTC (Wefelmeyer et al., 2015), and numerous other models (reviewed in Jamann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: A limitation of previous AIS plasticity studies is the post-hoc analysis of neuronal populations from different animals, which confines understanding of the temporal regulation of this process at the single-cell level.
source: However, a limitation of these studies is the post-hoc analysis of neuronal populations from different animals, which confines our understanding of the temporal regulation of this process at the single-cell level.
evidence: This describes a limitation of previous approaches.

claim: The ank-G-GFP model allows live imaging of the AIS under different physiological and pathophysiological conditions.
source: The ank-G-GFP model allows live imaging of the AIS under different physiological and pathophysiological conditions, generating a novel approach to the investigation and discovery of structure/function relationships and the temporal regulation of these processes in health and disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the model.

claim: Ankyrin-G plays a critical role in the establishment of the AIS and is responsible for the clustering of known AIS proteins, including voltage-gated ion channels, cell adhesion molecules, and inhibitory synaptic components.
source: Ankyrin-G plays a critical role in the establishment of the AIS and is responsible for the clustering of known AIS proteins, including voltage-gated ion channels, cell adhesion molecules, and inhibitory synaptic components (Jenkins et al., 2015; Nelson and Jenkins, 2017; Zhou et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The use of GFP-tagged native ankyrin-G as a molecular marker for the AIS allows early insight into AIS assembly in vivo.
source: Given this requirement for ankyrin-G to assemble the AIS, the use of GFP-tagged native ankyrin-G as a molecular marker for the AIS allows early insight into AIS assembly in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference about the utility of the model.

claim: Beyond the initial ankyrin-G-dependent assembly of the AIS, other components including voltage-gated sodium channels, βIV-spectrin, and neurofascin participate in AIS stability.
source: Beyond the initial ankyrin-G-dependent assembly of the AIS, other components of the AIS participate in its stability, including voltage-gated sodium channels, βIV-spectrin, and neurofascin (Leterrier et al., 2017; Lacas-Gervais et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Some components of the AIS, including voltage-gated sodium channels, alter their position along with ankyrin-G during homeostatic plasticity.
source: Some components of the AIS, including voltage-gated sodium channels, alter their position along with ankyrin-G during homeostatic plasticity (Grubb and Burrone, 2010), indicating a tight coupling of ankyrin-G and some binding partners.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Ankyrin-G-dependent GABAergic synapses can uncouple their AIS position from that of ankyrin-G.
source: Other AIS constituents, like ankyrin-G-dependent GABAergic synapses, can uncouple their AIS position from that of ankyrin-G (Wefelmeyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Post-hoc approaches have identified variability in nodes of Ranvier length, which could theoretically result in the regulation of action potential propagation velocity.
source: Similar to what has been observed with the AIS, post-hoc approaches have identified variability in noR length, which could theoretically result in the regulation of AP propagation velocity (Arancibia-Cárcamo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The ank-G-GFP mouse is a useful tool for monitoring size and position as well as glial interaction of nodes of Ranvier in vivo.
source: Here, we demonstrate efficient labeling of noR in ank-G-GFP mice, underlining the ank-G-GFP mouse as a useful tool for monitoring size and position as well as glial interaction of noR in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the model.

claim: Ankyrin-G is localized to the somatic membrane in mature neurons of the neocortex and hippocampus, where it regulates GABAergic synaptic density.
source: In addition to noR, ankyrin-G is also localized to the somatic membrane in mature neurons of the neocortex and hippocampus, where it regulates GABAergic synaptic density (Tseng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The 190 kDa isoform of ankyrin-G localizes to subdomains within dendritic spines, where it plays an important role in glutamate receptor stability and dendritic spine morphology.
source: Finally, the 190 kDa isoform of ankyrin-G localizes to subdomains within dendritic spines, where it plays an important role in glutamate receptor stability and dendritic spine morphology (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The ank-G-GFP mouse uses a carboxy-terminal GFP tag that would be present on all three major classes of Ank3 transcripts in the CNS (190, 270, and 480 kDa isoforms).
source: Since the ank-G-GFP mouse uses a carboxy-terminal GFP tag that would be present on all three major classes of Ank3 transcripts in the CNS (190, 270, and 480 kDa isoforms), future experiments with the ank-G-GFP line could examine ankyrin-G dynamics within dendritic spines during synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model.

claim: The ank-G-GFP reporter mouse, in combination with high temporal and spatial resolution imaging techniques, will move the AIS plasticity research field forward.
source: The ank-G-GFP reporter mouse, in combination with the high temporal and spatial resolution now obtained by e.g., voltage or calcium imaging, will move an entire research field forward.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the impact of the model.

claim: The added benefit of studying nodes of Ranvier and other ankyrin-G-dependent structures including those in the peripheral nervous system will open up avenues of investigations that have not been available to researchers.
source: In addition, the added benefit of also studying noR and other ankyrin-G-dependent structures including those in the peripheral nervous system, will open up avenues of investigations that have so far not been available to researchers.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the potential applications of the model.

claim: A FLEx cassette containing the last exon of Ank3 followed by a copy of the last exon of Ank3 fused with the coding sequence for eGFP in the reverse orientation was generated using standard molecular methods.
source: A FLEx cassette containing the last exon of Ank3 (ENSMUSE00001313132, exon 42) followed by a copy of the last exon of Ank3 fused with the coding sequence for eGFP in the reverse orientation was generated using standard molecular methods.
evidence: This describes the molecular construction of the targeting vector.

claim: The entire FLEx cassette was flanked by alternating loxP and lox2272 sites.
source: The entire cassette was flanked by alternating loxP and lox2272 sites.
evidence: This describes the molecular construction of the targeting vector.

claim: In the presence of Cre recombinase, the cassette orientation is irreversibly flipped by sequential recombination and excision of two of the lox sites.
source: In the presence of Cre recombinase, the cassette orientation is irreversibly flipped by sequential recombination and excision of two of the lox sites (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of Cre-dependent recombination, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The result of Cre recombination is the expression of an ankyrin-G-GFP fusion product from the endogenous locus only in cells expressing Cre recombinase.
source: The result is the expression of an ankyrin-G-GFP fusion product from the endogenous locus only in cells expressing Cre recombinase (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the outcome of Cre recombination, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The linker sequence between Ank3 and GFP is the same sequence used in previously described 190-, 270-, and 480-kDa ankyrin-G-GFP plasmids.
source: The linker sequence between Ank3 and GFP is the same sequence used in previously described 190-, 270-, and 480-kDa ankyrin-G-GFP plasmids (Kole and Stuart, 2012; Jenkins et al., 2015; Kizhatil and Bennett, 2004; Zhang and Bennett, 1998).
evidence: This describes the linker sequence with supporting citations.

claim: These ankyrin-G-GFP fusion products have been able to rescue all functions of ankyrin-G tested to date.
source: Importantly, these ankyrin-G-GFP fusion products have been able to rescue all functions of ankyrin-G tested to date, suggesting that the addition of GFP to the ankyrin-G carboxy-terminus does not affect ankyrin function (Jenkins et al., 2015; Tseng et al., 2015; Kizhatil and Bennett, 2004; Zhang and Bennett, 1998; He et al., 2014; He et al., 2012; Jenkins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The addition of GFP to the ankyrin-G carboxy-terminus does not affect ankyrin function.
source: Importantly, these ankyrin-G-GFP fusion products have been able to rescue all functions of ankyrin-G tested to date, suggesting that the addition of GFP to the ankyrin-G carboxy-terminus does not affect ankyrin function (Jenkins et al., 2015; Tseng et al., 2015; Kizhatil and Bennett, 2004; Zhang and Bennett, 1998; He et al., 2014; He et al., 2012; Jenkins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from rescue experiments cited.
